set.st: Cornelius and Stephen Horrigan distrusted banks and were said to have hidden money around their farm, which the AP put about 17 miles from Boscobel. On 11 Nov 1930 three men posing as hunters, with a well-dressed woman, came to the farm. They had asked earlier for permission to hunt on it. They killed Patrick Gorman, 65, and his son Paul, 18, visitors from Huron, South Dakota, and wounded both brothers (Stephen was shot through the arm and Cornelius's jaw was shattered), but fled without searching. Their sister Ellen, 75, kept house. The case was worked from Prairie du Chien, and a suspect was arrested at a Wauzeka roadhouse. Neighbors said there were many stories of buried treasure on the homestead, and many people had dug over the farm. The summer before, three men and a woman had been run off it while digging. Two local papers place the farm: the Grant County Herald (12 Nov 1930) says 'the Horrigan farm near Mt. Zion', and the Muscoda Leader-Press (27 Nov 1930) says 'between Mt. Zion and Soldiers Grove'. GNIS has Horrigan Ridge about 5 km NE of Mt. Zion, about 12 miles in a straight line from Boscobel. The Herald names the brothers as William and Cornelius, while the AP has Stephen. Pin: Horrigan Ridge (GNIS 1566706), sec. 35 T10N R3W, Crawford County, between Mt. Zion and Soldiers Grove. The exact farmstead needs a 1920s-30s Crawford plat. The 1914 Crawford County atlas spells the name Horgen and shows the brothers' land, about 760 acres, in secs. 25, 26, 35 and 36 of Clayton township. The papers gave 630 acres. The pin is now on the building by the road junction on C. M. Horgen's land. Placed: the c.1915 county plat shows Horrigan land across the north tier of sec. 2, Town of Scott, Crawford County, 16.7 miles due north of Boscobel, which fits '17 miles from Boscobel'. Private farm: ask permission. Local paper: the brothers distrusted banks and buried their money on the farm; robbers tried at least three times (c.1923 holdup took anywhere from a few hundred to $40,000 by differing reports; the 1930 attempt ended in murder); diggers worked the ground in all directions around the house. No find reported 1931-45. Private: permission. The Dial's account of the 11 Nov 1930 bandit raid on the Horrigan farm, in which two brothers were shot, names the suspects held in Chicago but says nothing of money hidden or found. The Muscoda Leader-Press of 13 Nov 1930 put the farm home '4 miles west of Tavera' and said the brothers had twice before defended the place against marauders drawn by reports of thousands of dollars in gold buried about the premises; they did not trust banks and had 'secreted their wealth in caches on the farm'. The 1922 papers fix the first holdup at 24 July 1922: about $40,000 taken from a trunk, $5,000 of it in gold, and the Dial already notes the family's habit of hiding money about the farm. Nothing from that robbery was reported recovered.
set.tovw: Lead grade B: period local papers from 1922 and 1930 and the AP give the hidden caches, three raids and the diggers; the farmstead is placed from the c.1915 plat and the 1938 aerial and confirmed by two independent bearings; no find reported.
